title: TypeScript basics
canDo: add types to JavaScript to catch bugs early

blocks.md: You have been writing JavaScript, and it has been working — mostly. But have you ever called a function with the wrong argument type, got `undefined` back, and spent twenty minutes wondering why? TypeScript exists precisely for that moment. It is a *layer on top of JavaScript* that reads your code before it runs and highlights the mistake with a red squiggle right in your editor. The bug never makes it to the browser. Phase 4 starts here because every lesson that follows — typed React props, typed API responses, typed routes — builds on the vocabulary you are about to learn.

blocks.canDo: add types to JavaScript to catch bugs early
blocks.md: By the end of this session you will be able to **add basic types to variables, function parameters, and return values**, **describe object shapes with interfaces**, and **explain why `any` defeats the purpose of TypeScript**. The learning happens inside the two curated resources below — work through them in order, then come back for the quiz.

**Four ideas to hold onto as you work through the resources:**

1. **Compile-time vs runtime.** TypeScript checks types *before* the code runs — that is why you see red squiggles in VS Code instead of `TypeError` in the console at 2 am.

2. **Basic types.** `string`, `number`, `boolean`, and arrays (`string[]` / `number[]`) cover the vast majority of everyday values.

3. **Interfaces describe object shapes.** An `interface User { name: string; age: number }` tells TypeScript exactly what properties an object must have — if you try to access `user.email` and it was not declared, TS flags it immediately.

4. **Avoid `any`.** Using `any` turns off type-checking for that value — it is the escape hatch that lets bugs back in. Prefer `unknown` when the type is genuinely unclear, then narrow it with a type guard.

### Total TypeScript — Beginner's TypeScript (free, interactive)

Matt Pocock's interactive tutorial runs entirely in the browser — no local setup needed. Work through **all exercises in the 'Beginner's TypeScript' section** (~50 min). Each exercise is a broken `.ts` file; your job is to fix the type error. The immediate red-squiggle feedback loop is the fastest way to internalise TS syntax.

> Note: the `/tutorials` section is **free**. Pro workshops (listed separately on the site) are paid — you do not need them for this lesson.
blocks.label: Open Total TypeScript — Beginner's TypeScript

### Net Ninja — TypeScript Tutorial playlist (YouTube, free)

The Net Ninja playlist gives you a clear talking-head walkthrough of the same concepts with live VS Code demos. Watch **videos 1–10** (~35 min). They cover project setup, basic types, objects, arrays, union types, and interfaces. Use this after the Total TypeScript exercises to solidify what you have seen interactively with a real editor workflow.
blocks.label: Open Net Ninja TypeScript playlist

blocks.md:
**Run TypeScript locally in minutes.** After the Net Ninja setup video, try it yourself:
```
npm create vite@latest my-ts-app -- --template vanilla-ts
cd my-ts-app
npm install
npm run dev
```
Open `src/main.ts` and intentionally write `const x: number = 'hello'` — save the file and watch the editor squiggle appear before you even switch to the browser.

questions.question: When does TypeScript catch type errors?
options: At runtime in the browser, the same time JavaScript would throw
Only when you run 'tsc --strict' manually from the terminal
Before the code runs — during compilation and in the editor as you type
After the first failing test in your test suite
questions.explanation: TypeScript's type-checker runs at compile time (and continuously in VS Code via the language server), so errors appear as red squiggles while you write the code — never reaching the browser.

questions.question: What is a TypeScript interface used for?
options: Defining a reusable CSS class that can be applied to components
Describing the required shape of an object — what properties it must have and their types
Declaring an abstract class that other classes must extend
Wrapping an async function so it returns a typed Promise automatically
questions.explanation: An interface (e.g. 'interface User { name: string; age: number }') tells TypeScript exactly which properties and types an object must conform to. Any object passed where a User is expected must satisfy that shape.

questions.question: Why should you avoid using the 'any' type in TypeScript?
options: It makes the code run slower because TypeScript cannot optimise unknown values
It is a syntax error in strict mode and will prevent compilation
It disables type-checking for that value, allowing the same bugs TypeScript was meant to catch
It causes interfaces to be ignored at runtime by the JavaScript engine
questions.explanation: Assigning 'any' tells TypeScript 'trust me, I know what this is' — effectively opting out of type safety for that value. Bugs can silently re-enter exactly where you thought you had coverage.

blocks.md: TypeScript checks your types *before* the code runs, turning silent runtime bugs into visible editor squiggles. You now have the core vocabulary: primitive types (`string`, `number`, `boolean`, arrays), interfaces for object shapes, typed function signatures, and the rule of thumb to avoid `any`. In the next lesson you will carry these skills directly into React — typing component props and hook return values so your UI components become self-documenting and bug-resistant.
